无为 (wuwei) is the Taoist idea of action that does not force. Water does not argue with the rock; it goes around it, takes the shape of its container, and over time it still cuts the canyon. And when it has to, water crashes.

WUWEI applies that to an agent team:

Water WUWEI Takes the shape of the container Reads each repository's own process (its PR template, spec engine, default branch, protection rules) and fills only the gaps Flows around the rock A blocked item waits visibly on the board; the team moves to the next one without asking you Finds the lowest path The right path is the cheapest one: a ready PR body, a verdict skeleton, one command to see what is missing Still when undisturbed When the evidence is complete, WUWEI says nothing Crashes when it must A few doors hold absolutely

docs.title: An auditor with narrow police powers
docs.text:
WUWEI is a process auditor. An auditor does not run the company and does not stop all work to prevent bad behaviour. It knows what good looks like, reads the records, names what is missing, and has the authority to stop a small number of things that cannot be undone.

That stance is the main design decision, and it came from experience. WUWEI 0.x prescribed every step: a command returned the next command, and the model executed it. The model, working in its own harness, kept finding valid paths the protocol did not model (resuming a seat with SendMessage, writing a file through the shell, merging in the browser). Each one put the protocol's records out of sync, and each fix modelled one more path. Twenty days, 186 bug fixes and 33,000 lines later, the friction was the product.

Evidence does not have that problem. It does not matter how a test got into the diff, only that it is there. It does not matter how a review was launched, only that an independent reviewer wrote it at this head and nobody edited it since.

docs.title: Responsible autonomy
docs.text:
The goal is autonomy you can trust, which needs two things at once:

  • Fewer mistakes. The evidence contract, the gates, the doors and the learning loop each exist to catch a class of mistake before it ships, or to stop it from shipping twice.
  • Less of your attention. The model decides everything it can undo cheaply, records its assumptions, and asks only what is yours. Questions the process can answer are sent back.

Autonomy here is not a switch. It grows when results are good (fewer escaped defects, calibrated confidence) and shrinks when they are not, by itself: see the error budget.

docs.title: No wrappers
docs.text: WUWEI never stands between the model and its tools. There is no wuwei merge the model must use instead of gh pr merge, no wuwei worktree instead of git worktree. The model uses git, gh and the repository's tools directly. WUWEI's own commands only read and record.

docs.title: Budgets keep it small
docs.text: The runtime is standard-library Python held to 3,800 lines by a test, and the configuration has six keys. A change that would break a budget must delete something first. Process tools tend to grow until they are the problem; the budget is the defence.

docs.title: The team and its charters
docs.text: Role Does Why it is a separate role planner your session: plans with the lead, launches seats, follows the board, asks you what is yours one place where your attention is spent lead discovery, readiness, scope, tier, ranking, red-teaming the plan deciding what to build is a different skill from building it builder one item, test first, in its own branch and worktree small, isolated changes are easier to review and undo sentinel-arch architecture gate: conformance to the written design, coupling, contracts, quality attributes, budgets coupling and contracts erode quietly sentinel-quality quality gate, on a different model than the builder when the model table puts the rest on one tests that do not test, code that should not exist sentinel-security security gate trust boundaries need a reviewer who looks only at them sentinel-goal goal gate (full tier) building the wrong thing well is still wrong shepherd PRs from raise to merge: reviewers, threads, CI, conflicts, the evidence comment PRs die of neglect, not of bad code steward the retro at each checkpoint someone must learn from the day without being in it

docs.title: Charters are the one source
docs.text:
Each role's conduct is a charter in charters/: _common.md for everyone, _common-authoring.md for roles that write for people, _gate.md for the sentinels, and one file per role. The agents in agents/ are generated from them (wuwei agents build) with a reviewed tool grant per role (agents/allowlist.json), and a test fails if they drift.

Why: a rule written in two places drifts. The charter is where a rule lives; the agent is how the harness receives it.

The charters hold only what every workspace needs. A lesson about one repository's code lives in that repository (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) and in the workspace's .wuwei/standards.md, never in a charter. Tests hold the charters to the plain-tone rule (no sentence over 35 words) and each generated agent under a word ceiling, so the set cannot grow by accretion.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
The sentinels review the diff, the requirement and the running code, never the builder's summary. They run probes and mutants in a scratch copy of the tree at the head they review. Their verdicts count only when attested.

At least one gate per head runs on a different model than the builder, so the reviews do not share every blind spot. Each seat's model and effort come from one table in the planner charter, drawn from Anthropic's guidance; the planner follows it and may depart with a reason.

Why: a reviewer who shares the author's assumptions finds the author's mistakes only by luck.

docs.title: Rounds that converge
docs.text:
A surviving mutant blocks only when the gate can name a concrete bad input it lets through and the harm it does; an equivalent or unexploitable mutant is a low note with the missing test. From the third round on, a gate blocks only on what the last fix changed, and test-only findings on code already judged correct go to one combined final round. Two fix rounds without a pass on the code itself park the item for a rethink.

Why: a gate that finds a new unpinned quantifier on the same unchanged regex each round costs a dozen seats and buys nothing; a defect is a bad input, not a missing test.

docs.title: Seats cannot ask you
docs.text:
Seats have no question tool. Only the planner reaches you, and only with an owner-class question.

Why: one voice, batched, with a recommendation, instead of every agent interrupting you.

docs.title: Standards travel with the brief
docs.text: Seats do not see the session's context, so the planner passes each seat the lines of .wuwei/standards.md for its role: the defects this workspace has seen escape, the rules the retro promoted.

docs.title: The day
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    goals([goals: the direction]) --> pass
    pass --> view{{"plan view: you approve"}}
    pass["plan pass<br/>(any number per day)"]
    view --> work["builders, gates, shepherd"]
    work --> evidence{"evidence<br/>complete?"}
    evidence -- gaps --> work
    evidence -- yes --> merge["merge"]
    merge --> checkpoint["checkpoint<br/>report + retro"]
    checkpoint -- "standards, vaccines, proposals" --> pass

docs.title: Goals and the plan view
docs.text:
Your goals live in .wuwei/goals.md: outcome, measure, target, date and priority. They set the direction the lead ranks against.

Each plan pass ends with the plan as a picture: wuwei plan view writes .wuwei/plan.html (light and dark, readable on a phone) with the ranking formula, the estimated build hours (one WSJF size point is one hour), and a card per goal with its items by score. Then one question: approve or change. New items wait on the board as awaiting plan approval until you approve; work you already approved keeps running.

Why: you own the direction and the trade-offs, and you should see them at a glance, not in a two-kilobyte paragraph. One picture, one answer.

docs.title: Plan passes
docs.text:
A plan pass (/wuwei-run) adds, drops or re-ranks items in .wuwei/plan.json. Run it as often as the day needs: in the morning, when the queue runs dry, when you add something, when priorities shift. The plan is a running queue that carries across days, not a daily document.

The lead does the thinking in a pass. It reads every source it can reach (issues, red checks, review threads, follow-ups, regressions), returns only ready candidates (a promise, acceptance scenarios, the repository and files), and red-teams the plan: it names the riskiest item and the cheapest way to learn early whether it works, and ranks that learning first.

Why: days change. A plan you can only make once goes stale by lunch, and a team that cannot re-plan either stalls or improvises.

docs.title: Ranking
docs.text:
The configured framework ranks the queue, never a hand order.

  • WSJF (default): value to the goal, time criticality, risk reduction, each on 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, divided by job size.
  • RICE: reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort.

Every score carries one line of evidence. Why: a ranking you can read the reasons for is a ranking you can correct.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
Work already in progress follows Kanban flow policy, not the last event:

  1. Class of service, most urgent first: expedite, fixed-date, standard, intangible. Set it with wuwei plan add --class. An item is standard by default and fixed-date when its goal has a date. Only one expedite item is open at a time; a second is refused, and so is a restore of one.
  2. Closest to done, right to left: ready to merge, owner review, gates, fix round, building.
  3. Age, oldest first.

Each board row shows its class and the hours since its last event. A PR idle 4 hours with no live seat on its item shows stale with its last event, first in its class. A WSJF item's time criticality rises one Fibonacci step per day its first PR is open.

An item can wait on another: wuwei plan add <id> --after <other>. While the other is open, the board shows waiting on <other>, the Stop reminder leaves it out, and the other's score adds the waiting item's cost of delay. A wait that would close a cycle (an item waiting on itself, or on an item that already waits on it) is refused.

Why: attention goes to whatever moved last, so an old draft starves. Finishing what is closest to done, in class order, keeps work flowing.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
A close (/wuwei-close) writes the report for the day so far and launches the steward for the retro. It locks nothing: the next plan pass reopens the day. A second checkpoint starts with what changed since the first. There is no end time.

Why: you stop when you stop. A checkpoint gives you the picture whenever you want it without pretending the day has a fixed shape.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
Each item has a tier that sets how much evidence it needs:

Tier For Gates light a trivial, local change quality standard the default arch, quality, security full contracts, schemas, boundaries, auth, secrets, agent tooling, infrastructure arch, quality, security, goal

When unsure, the lead goes up. A repository over its error budget raises every tier one step, and a light item whose code touches a trust path is raised to standard.

docs.title: Work in progress
docs.text: Open work should keep moving without you nudging it: PRs with a red check or an unanswered review, a question in a Slack thread, a stale branch. WUWEI does this with a watch pass and owed replies.

docs.title: The watch pass
docs.text:
/wuwei-watch is one pass over everything in flight:

  1. Owed replies, oldest due first, answered in their own thread.
  2. New asks from the connected chat and tracker tools, recorded as owed replies.
  3. Open PRs, as the shepherd charter says: CI, conflicts, threads, reviewers, stale branches, merges (or auto-merge while only CI runs).
  4. One line recorded (wuwei watch --record). Nothing changed means nothing is said.

Why: a team that only moves when you ask is not autonomous. The watch is the habit of checking on your own work, done on a clock instead of on your memory.

docs.title: Flow: finish before starting
docs.text:
Starting work feels like progress; finishing it is progress. Too many items open at once means none of them closes, and too many seats at once slows every turn. So the planner works a Kanban limit, as advice:

  • WIP limit, default 4. An item is in progress while it has an open PR, a running builder or a registered Codex job. A new item starts only while fewer than four are in progress across the workspace. Fix rounds, gates, shepherd work and merges on open PRs always come first.
  • Seat ceiling, default 8. At most eight seats run at once in a session.
  • You decide. Ask for more and the planner tells you the cost once (slower turns, rate limits sooner, more notifications in the session), then does it. It records your number as a dated WIP limit: <n> or Seat ceiling: <n> line in .wuwei/standards.md, which holds until you change it. WUWEI advises; it never refuses a start.
  • The numbers learn. At each close the steward measures peak live seats, peak items in progress, starts against merges per day, and tool-call duration by live seat count. It re-derives the WIP limit by Little's law (merges per day times PR lead time) and the ceiling from where tool calls slow down, and proposes a change with those numbers.

/wuwei-close also does housekeeping for what the session started: it removes clean worktrees of finished items, stops its own background tasks, clears finished seats' scratch folders, and reports the cache size. A process the session did not start is named to you once, never killed.

Why: a smaller batch in flight finishes sooner, and a limit you can see is one you can change.

docs.title: Who runs it
docs.text:
The plugin runs no background process; Claude Code's own scheduling does:

Where How Your machine /loop 20m /wuwei-watch in the session Claude Code cloud an hourly routine running /wuwei-watch in the workspace repository, and a GitHub PR subscription on each open PR so reviews and CI wake the session between passes

Hooks cannot wake an idle session: they fire only on events inside a running one. They still do their part: the Stop hook does not let a turn end while someone waits on a reply, and a send closes the reply it answers.

docs.title: Owed replies
docs.text:
wuwei owe <thread link> "<what was asked>" --who <name> --within 4h records that someone is waiting. It sits on the board as reply owed to <name> in <thread>, due <time>, and as overdue once past due. When the team sends a message into that thread through a connected tool, the PostToolUse hook closes the reply by itself: the evidence is the send, not someone remembering to tick a box.

The report shows replies owed, closed, open and overdue, and the median response time.

docs.title: Review requests
docs.text: When .wuwei/standards.md names where the team asks for reviews (`Review requests: Slack

docs.title: eng-reviews`), every ready PR the team raises owes one post there with its link. Until a send
docs.text:
naming the PR is recorded, or someone other than the author has reviewed it, the PR carries review not requested in <place> on the board, and the Stop hook does not let the turn end on it. It is a duty, not a safety gap: it never holds the merge. A post made outside the session is recorded with wuwei sent owner/repo#n <link to the post>. A 0.34 workspace's review_channel becomes that line on upgrade.

PRs raised by hand count too. An open PR by the session's identity on a configured repository, opened in the last seven days with no plan link, shows on the board as unplanned with its gaps, so it is shepherded like any other.

Why: a PR nobody was asked to review waits silently; asking is part of raising it.

Why: people waiting on an answer are the work in progress that hurts most when forgotten, and the easiest to forget, because no CI turns red when a question goes unanswered.
